title: Flint's ML-guided lead-pipe search hits 70% through 2017; hit rate falls to 15% after the model is dropped
summary: A University of Michigan XGBoost and active-learning model guided Flint's FAST Start digs; 6,228 of 8,833 homes inspected through 2017 had lead pipes replaced (70%), versus 15% in 2018 without it.
account: From summer 2016 Jacob Abernethy, Eric Schwartz and colleagues at the University of Michigan worked with Flint's FAST Start service-line replacement program. They built a statistical model (gradient-boosted trees in XGBoost with a hierarchical Bayesian spatial layer) and an active-learning procedure, ActiveRemediation. They chose which homes to inspect and replace (KDD 2018 paper, arXiv 1806.10692). The paper reports 91.6% accuracy on a 1,606-home holdout set. By September 2017, 4,419 hazardous service lines were replaced, with the composition of 6,506 homes identified. The Atlantic (Alexis Madrigal, 3 January 2019) reported that through 2017 workers inspected 8,833 homes and replaced pipes at 6,228, a 70 percent rate. It quoted program head Michael McDaniel saying accuracy was above 80 percent in late 2017. The City hired AECOM in 2018, which discarded the model's predictions. By mid-December 2018, 10,531 properties were explored and only 1,567 digs found lead, a 15 percent hit rate. In a court filing Schwartz estimated 4,964 to 6,119 homes with hazardous lines remained. The date used is the KDD paper's publication date. The model-guided phase ran through 2017.
purpose: The model and active-learning rules were built to predict which Flint homes had lead or galvanized service lines and to direct inspections and replacements. The improved hit rate was the intended use.
system: ActiveRemediation: XGBoost classifier with hierarchical Bayesian spatial model and importance-weighted active learning for service-line selection
developer: University of Michigan team (Jacob Abernethy, Alex Chojnacki, Arya Farahi, Eric Schwartz, Jared Webb)
deployer: City of Flint FAST Start service-line replacement program
taxonomy_note: The public-health good of lead removal is the end; the documented gain is the hit rate per excavation.

ratings.reason: Households had lead or galvanized lines replaced faster under model-guided targeting (6,228 replacements through 2017). Outcomes are documented in aggregate, no individual named.
FAST Start's hit rate was 70 percent through 2017, above 80 percent in late 2017 per McDaniel, against 15 percent in 2018 without the model. The KDD paper reports 91.6% holdout accuracy.
Flint's court-ordered lead-removal mandate was served faster while the model guided digs. The Atlantic reports thousands of homes kept lead pipes longer after it was dropped.

ai_role.statement: The model's predictions guided which homes were excavated through 2017. The hit-rate collapse after AECOM discarded them supports its contribution. The comparison is observational and confounded by the City's simultaneous shift to digging across wards. Sources are the makers' peer-reviewed paper and an independent news report with named sources.

produced_by: Digitized historical parcel and service-line records plus water-sample data
Contractor hydrovac inspections and replacements feeding labels back to the model
City officials who followed the model's recommendations when selecting homes
must_hold: Decision-makers continue to use the predictions (the 2018 hit rate fell when they were dropped)
Inspection results are returned to the model to update it
Equity constraints that do not override targeting entirely

headline: ActiveRemediation guides Flint digs to a 70% lead-pipe hit rate
metric: 6,228 of 8,833 homes inspected through 2017 had lead pipes replaced (70%)

comparator.against: home selection by the new contractor in 2018 without the model
comparator.before: they were only finding lead at about 15 of those
comparator.quote: What we found was actually for every hundred homes they were going to with the intention of replacing those lines, they were only finding lead at about 15 of those. So, instead of 80-some-odd percent, it went down to 15% in just a matter of a few months.

later.note: Under the court settlement in Concerned Pastors for Social Action v. Khouri, Flint agreed to use the Schwartz-Abernethy model again to select homes for excavation in 2019.
later.quote: The parties to the settlement in Concerned Pastors for Social Action v. Khouri agreed that the city will use a statistical model developed by Dr. Eric Schwartz of the University of Michigan and Dr. Jacob Abernethy at the Georgia Institute of Technology to guide its selection of homes for service line excavations in 2019.
